candidates.title: Interpreting a recent acceleration in pretraining loss
candidates.author: Ajeya Cotra, Jean-Stanislas Denain, Tom Cunningham
candidates.event_date: 2026-11-22 (OpenAI 'Perplexity and Intelligence' post by Jakub Pachocki, https://openai.com/index/perplexity-and-intelligence/, dated Nov 22 on page)
candidates.what_changed: OpenAI published base-model log-perplexity for 13 models since GPT-3.5 on a fixed held-out set from its own codebase; METR responds with how to interpret the apparent ~7x acceleration since early 2026 and what extra data developers should publish.
candidates.mechanism: Log-perplexity on a fixed held-out corpus tracks pretraining progress; METR converts it into 'effective compute' under a shared scaling law and lists confounders (overfitting/leakage of the codebase corpus, release date vs pretraining end date, growth in compute/labor/experiment compute vs AI uplift).
candidates.evidence_quality: Medium. Interpretation piece by a credible eval org; underlying data is a single company's internal metric on one corpus (its own codebase). METR explicitly says it has no consensus view.
candidates.independent_confirmation: METR says Microsoft has since published the same metric for its own models using OpenAI's dataset (linked to a Mustafa Suleyman X post; UNVERIFIED, not fetched). OpenAI's source post fetched and dated Nov 22; its log-perplexity anchors: GPT-3.5 ~0.99, GPT-4 ~0.91, recent models below 0.8.
candidates.relevance: Medium-low for practitioners directly; high for forecasting/eval readers. Useful angle: a lab-published metric whose single held-out corpus is code, and how to read vendor-published progress metrics critically (ask for multiple held-out sets, pretraining-end dates, resource inputs).
candidates.overlap_with_prior: Adjacent to Edition 4's METR Q4 capability update (metr.org/blog/2026-11-20-q4-2026-capability-update, already used) and METR's Anthropic AI R&D acceleration assessment; new URL and new topic (pretraining loss).
candidates.summary: OpenAI recently published the base-model log-perplexity of 13 models trained since GPT-3.5, measured on a fixed held-out dataset sourced from OpenAI's own codebase. METR: since early 2026 loss has been falling about seven times faster than in 2022 through 2025; at the current pace OpenAI would cover the GPT-3.5 to GPT-4.1 drop (which took three years) in about six and a half months. This is notable because under standard (Chinchilla) scaling laws each 10x compute buys a smaller loss drop, and there is an irreducible floor, so progress in loss should slow. METR staff disagree on how to reconcile this with the lack of comparable acceleration in OpenAI's benchmark scores (e.g., Epoch's ECI). Three readings: (1) the data overstates progress via overfitting, e.g., parts of the codebase leaking into training; (2) benchmarks are the better measure of real-world capability and perplexity only an input, so forecasts change little, although to the extent AI drove the pretraining gains it signals AI's future contribution to the whole training pipeline; (3) perplexity is a deeper capability measure and an acceleration in real-world capability will follow; some interpretations imply broad-based acceleration over the next six months. METR says no frontier developer had previously published multi-year pretraining loss on a fixed held-out set, and urges all developers to do so (Microsoft reportedly has, using OpenAI's dataset). Requests: (a) log-perplexity on other, very different held-out corpora (e.g., books), ideally pre-2022 to avoid AI-generated text, covering code, scientific writing and prose, eventually maintained by a third party for cross-developer comparison; (b) the rough date each model's pretraining run ended, since release dates can lag and a shrinking lag would inflate the apparent acceleration, and to attribute gains to AI uplift; (c) how pretraining compute, labor spending and experiment compute changed. Footnotes: assuming all OpenAI models are on one scaling law with irreducible loss 0.3-0.6, effective compute grew roughly 8-10x faster (in OOM/year) since early 2026 than in 2022-2025, though newer recipes likely follow different laws; architectural changes such as looped transformers may lower perplexity more than they improve downstream capability; OpenAI's footnote attributes the acceleration 'mostly to long term research and compute investments, and only in a smaller part to automation' but notes 'meaningful design contributions coming from AI' for recent models; METR's Anthropic assessment estimated perhaps ~80% of the October 2026 acceleration there is due to AI; capability scales like ECI, MCI and time horizon are sensitive to statistical assumptions and near-saturated benchmarks.

candidates.title: The Pragmatic Engineer Essay Challenge: Category Winners (Part 1)
candidates.author: Gergely Orosz, Jessica Salmon, Ivan Klaric
candidates.paywall: Free to read in full as fetched (Deepdives section; opens with a Black Friday subscription promo). Linked essays are on external sites (Substack, personal blogs, LinkedIn, Google Docs, X).
candidates.what_changed: Excerpts from three category winners and runners-up of a reader essay contest on how AI changed building software, with first-hand before/after data from teams of 1 to 700 people.
candidates.mechanism: First-person experience reports: code review collapse when reviews become optional, EMs returning to hands-on work with 6-8 parallel agent sessions, solo builders running agent-driven bug-fix batches, verification-step design as the core skill.
candidates.evidence_quality: Low-medium: self-reported anecdotes and self-measured metrics (LoC, commits, PRs); curated by editors; 'no AI' writing rule for the contest. Useful as practitioner texture, not as measurement.
candidates.independent_confirmation: None; individual accounts. Charts attributed to Weave (engineering analytics) in the HoneyBook essay (UNVERIFIED).
candidates.relevance: Medium-high for practitioner readers: concrete failure modes (review collapse, non-engineers shipping 10k-line PRs, quality regression) and practices (verification steps, parallel checkouts, skills with team context).
candidates.overlap_with_prior: Grand-prize essay 'tale of two eras' was a Nov 3 post (not in prior URLs list). Edition 3 used Pragmatic Engineer's Harjot Gill software-factories/code-review podcast; HoneyBook 'code review collapse' excerpt advances that theme with a counterpoint.
candidates.summary: Contest launched for the newsletter's fifth birthday (September); $10,000 grand prize went to Neil Kakkar's 'How software engineering changed: a tale of two eras'; six category winners got $2,500 each; Part 1 covers three categories and links ~40 more essays. (1) 'What happens when AI writes all the code?' Winner: Anton Zaides (EM at HoneyBook, 13-year-old startup, ~$500M raised; team of seven on financial products). Three repos with different review policies: shared ai-workflows (every PR reviewed by at least two people), atlas-vibe frontend (barely any PRs, vibe-coded, improving repo skills), backend (optional reviews). With optional reviews, engineers stopped requesting them; Zaides notes review creates peer pressure to understand your own code, and 'in the span of a couple of months, we dropped from two people reviewing and understanding the code, to zero', yielding 'a buggy codebase full of duplications and non-optimal patterns'. In June 2026 a designer opened a 10k-line PR with hacky code and dummy data in place of backend calls. Zaides went from ~1 PR/week (Oct 2025-Mar 2026) to 20+, runs 6-8 parallel sessions (up from 2-3); team ditched a home-grown agentic solution for 'Eve by Vercel' (UNVERIFIED product name, from excerpt). Runners-up: Paul D'Ambra (PostHog) on engineers as 'software machinists' who build tooling and inspect samples; predicts CI and review change next; PostHog built deep review agents. Kira Howe (Seeq) on CI/observability changes. Marc-André Moreau (CTO, Devolutions, 250 people): voluntary departure package for those not wanting to go AI-native; a migration estimated at ~3 years per platform done in under one for Windows and Linux; app with 1,500 screens; internal hackathon produced 60 useful skills; AI spend grew to $2M/year. Carlo Beschi (Treatwell, 700 staff): 16 changes incl. more migrations, prototyping in Claude Design, 80/20 rule, role blurring. Bruno Felix (XEO360, 8 people): shift from 'rowing' to 'steering'. Shout-out: Krzysztof Maliszewski surveyed 40 Coralogix engineers, half admit being 'addicted to agents'. (2) Solo builders. Winner: David Veszelovszki (ex-Sourcegraph; built Cmdr file manager): 194 LoC/active day at Sourcegraph 2022-2025 (~100/calendar day) vs Cmdr at 1.4M LoC in 10 months (>4,500 LoC/day; 12,000/day last 30 days), 1,674 changelog entries (~40/month Jan-Feb to 230-350/month Aug-Oct), 12,003 commits (~15/workday in Jan to ~160 in Oct), 67 releases. Setup: Claude Code with Opus 5.5 medium, single 20x Max plan, few-line prompts, no specs, no skills, almost no rule files, no code reviews, manual QA at the end, Claude-maintained infra; '100% of the product level, 0% of the code level'. On 2026-10-01 closed 42 GitHub issues by asking Claude to pick ~10 small tickets, use subagents, merge, push and 'make CI happy', four rounds; UI copy always returned to him for edit. S3 connect feature: 50k LoC in two days, tested with seven providers. Runners-up: Mayhul Arora (Heartbeat, 4 people, $1M+/month bookings) expects 2-3 people maintaining the 'core agentic factory' (data fetching patterns, CI, design system, scheduled agents, dev environments) while others build features; Joshua Warren (sole developer at Blend Supply, aerospace paint) built a software factory on the 'Oh My Pi' harness, agents attend weekly status meetings, deploys 50+ times/day vs once a month, replaced several agencies. (3) Reflections. Winner: Jacob Bartlett (Granola) on monthly workflow shifts per model release (Dec 2025 GPT-5.2/Opus 4.5 through Sep 2026 GPT-6 Astra/Fable 5.1/Opus 5.5); skills: designing verification steps, planning alongside agents, parallelizing across multiple git checkouts, context switching; shipped 'Meeting Bar' in 20% time via a background agent tab. Runners-up: Daniel Silva (Coverflex), Ben Cohen (Substack), Max Oliinyk (F-Secure; Claude Code with team-specific skills; rarely hits limits except 5h limit with high effort/expensive model/dynamic workflows), Fawziyah A (Imprint) on juniors learning faster. Shout-outs include Carly Rector '5 new types of failures in AI-native development' (https://carlyrector.substack.com/p/5-new-types-of-failures-in-ai-native) and Sara Spagnoletto (Google/Waze) opening 3x as many PRs with Antigravity. Takeaway: most recall the step change with Opus 4.5/4.6 and new problems from code volume and non-engineers coding. Part 2 to follow.

candidates.title: Import AI 482: Huawei kernel benchmarks; airborne drone detection; and a national lab's AI science benchmark
candidates.author: Jack Clark
candidates.pub_date: 2026-11-23 14:11 UTC (confirmed on page; also mirrored at https://jack-clark.net/2026/11/23/import-ai-482-huawei-kernel-benchmarks-airborne-drone-detection-and-a-national-labs-ai-science-benchmark/)
candidates.event_date: Underlying papers: SciResearch-Eval arXiv 2611.21541 submitted 2026-11-16; AscendGYM arXiv 2611.17621 v1 2026-11-13, v2 2026-11-20
candidates.what_changed: Issue 482 is out (after Edition 4's 08:00 UTC Nov 23 cutoff). Most practitioner-relevant item: LLNL's SciResearch-Eval, which scores whether agents report calibrated 95% intervals when their tool (a simulator) is silently wrong. Also AscendGYM (cost-aware kernel-optimization benchmark with a speedup-per-token metric, harness comparisons), Noeri neolab launch, A2A-UAV dataset.
candidates.mechanism: SciResearch-Eval: agent designs 4 extra experiments under budgets, fits a heat-conduction simulator that may be under-resolved or missing physics, reports conductivity, heat capacity and rear heat-transfer coefficient with 95% intervals, scored with proper scoring rules against exact ground truth. AscendGYM: 48 Ascend NPU kernels at three difficulty levels with real-workload shapes; model and model-harness evaluation modes; Speedup-Token Score (STS) jointly weighs speedup and token cost.
candidates.evidence_quality: SciResearch-Eval: medium-high (93 held-out tasks, 9 models, 2,511 episodes, pre-registered fresh split and effort ablation, environment/graders/harness released) per arXiv abstract. AscendGYM: technical report; harness ranking claims come from Clark's summary (per-model numbers not verified in paper).
candidates.independent_confirmation: SciResearch-Eval numbers confirmed on arXiv abstract page (arXiv:2611.21541). AscendGYM 48 kernels / STS metric confirmed on arXiv abstract (2611.17621); model ordering (Opus 5 > GPT-5.6 > GLM-5.3; Claude Code best absolute; GPT better in Codex; Opus 5 more token-hungry) is from Import AI only, UNVERIFIED in paper.
candidates.relevance: High for evals/reliability: 'a confident wrong number is worse than honest uncertainty'; asking for wider intervals doesn't fix calibration; stating a strategy helps scores but not coverage; more reasoning effort unlocks latent correction at 13-31x token cost. AscendGYM relevant to cost-aware eval design (speedup per token) and harness-vs-model comparisons.
candidates.overlap_with_prior: Import AI 481 was used in Edition 2 (different content). Calibration/'tool answer may be wrong' theme connects to Edition 2's 'Check the tool's answer in the harness'.
candidates.summary: Issue 482 confirmed published Nov 23, 2026 14:11 UTC on Substack and jack-clark.net. Items: (1) AscendGYM (Shenzhen Loop Area Institute / SLAI): benchmark for whether an agent can further improve a correct kernel for a target workload within budget while preserving correctness; initial suite of 48 kernels across three difficulty levels, test cases with dtypes and tensor shapes from real training and inference workloads; AscendForge environment with unified compilation, correctness checking, performance measurement and feedback; built-in harness with search orchestration and experience accumulation; new Speedup-Token Score (STS). Per Clark: best model Opus 5, then GPT-5.6, then GLM-5.3; tested in Claude Code, Codex and OpenCode; Claude Code gives best absolute scores and GLM does well in it, GPT does well in Codex; Opus 5 more token-hungry, GPT-5.6 more token-efficient. Clark frames it as an ingredient for Chinese RSI and relevant to export controls. Code: https://github.com/SLAI-AITP/AscendGYM. (2) SciResearch-Eval (Lawrence Livermore; Weston, Torres Contreras, Gongora; arXiv 2611.21541, LLNL-JRNL-2026874): agent gets a sample, a heat-conduction simulator, one heating experiment, budgets for four more self-designed experiments, compute for simulations/fits, and an action cap; must report three properties with 95% intervals and predict a measurement it may not run. Hidden: simulator may be under-resolved, physically wrong (temperature-dependent conductivity, glued joint, front-face radiation, side heat loss) or fed uninformative data. Held-out split: 93 tasks, 9 models, 2,511 episodes. Models handle procedural traps, but when physics is missing most report wrong values at stated 95% confidence: intervals contain truth 20-62% of the time vs 94% for GPT-6 Astra and 99% for Claude Fable 5.2. At default effort Claude 5.5 models rarely diagnose missing physics (Opus 35% of episodes vs Astra 66%); Astra and Fable design experiments where the flawed simulator is accurate (e.g., gentle heating). Asking for wider intervals does not help; stating the strategy improves interval scores 1.6-2.5x (replicated on a pre-registered fresh split) but coverage barely moves. Pre-registered effort ablation: at maximum effort Opus improves more than tenfold and is no longer detectably behind Astra-at-default, but with 13-31x more reasoning; older and open-weight models gain nothing. Fable 5.2 most accurate at default (interval score 1.9x better than Astra) but writes 6x the tokens and falls short at Astra's token count. Environment, graders, harness and leaderboard released (https://btwestyo.github.io/sciresearch-eval/). (3) Noeri: Stanford's Yejin Choi and Carlos Guestrin launch a 'plural intelligence' neolab, raised $110m; themes: continual/test-time training, self-distillation, small-model orchestration of other models and tools beating frontier models at lower cost (claims from announcement, few technical details). (4) A2A-UAV: 105,263 samples, RGB + panoramic + thermal + RF time-frequency + mmWave radar + metadata, three locations, day/night, 15 target drones from 13 commercial models, 271 archives ~2.5 TB. (5) Tech Tale on 'machine hermeneutics'. Reader comment (Aryan Pegwar) applies the calibration point to agent products where guesses and checked facts look identical.
